61	
62	Every export's sound goes through a master limiter, whatever you choose here. See [Export loudness](/export/loudness/).
63	
64	## Unavailable controls
65	
66	A control the chosen format can't use is greyed out rather than hidden, and its value isn't sent. So a greyed-out control never affects the file.
67	
68	| Control | Available on |
69	| --- | --- |
70	| **Dynamic Range:** | HEVC 10-bit (MP4), AV1 (MP4), AV1 (WebM), VP9 (WebM), ProRes 422 (MOV) and ProRes 4444 (MOV). On any other format it's greyed out and shows **SDR version**, which is what that format writes. |
71	| **Speed:** | AV1 (MP4) and AV1 (WebM) |
72	| **Size:**, **Frame rate:** and **Burn in timecode** | Every format but the three audio-only ones |
73	| **Quality:** | Every format but ProRes, WAV, AIFF, GIF and APNG |
74	| **Bit depth:** | Audio only (WAV) and Audio only (AIFF) |
75	| **Stems:** | The three audio-only formats |
76	| **Loudness:** | Every format but GIF and APNG |
77	
78	**Speed:**, **Bit depth:** and **Stems:** go on showing your last choice while they're greyed out, and it comes back when you pick a format that uses it.
79	
80	**Range:** doesn't depend on the format. It's greyed out when the project has no in/out range. It's greyed out inside a nest too, even when the nest has a range, and its tooltip says why: an export writes the whole timeline, so it can't use a range that belongs to the nest. Leave the nest with <kbd>⌘↑</kbd> and set a range on the timeline.
81	
82	## The readout line
83	
84	The line under the controls says what size, rate and length the file will have. These are the file's real numbers, so a GIF's fitted size or an evened edge shows here.
85	
86	| Kind of file | The readout looks like |
87	| --- | --- |
88	| A movie | `1920 × 1080 · 30 fps · 00:01:12:05` |
89	| An audio-only file | `Audio only · 00:01:12.200` |
90	| A GIF or APNG | The movie line, followed by `· 360 frames, no audio` |
91	
92	When the sheet can't work out a valid file, the readout says what to fix and **Export…** and **Add to Queue** are greyed out. An empty custom field gives "Type a width and a height, or pick a size from the list." or "Type a loudness target in LUFS, or pick one from the list."
93	
94	## Estimated time
95	
96	On AV1 (MP4), AV1 (WebM), VP9 (WebM) and VP9 with Alpha (WebM) a second line estimates how long the export will take, for example `Estimated time: about 25 s`. The other formats show no estimate.
97	
98	| How long | It reads |
99	| --- | --- |
100	| Under a minute | Seconds, in steps of 5: `about 25 s` |
101	| Under an hour | Whole minutes: `about 3 min` |
102	| An hour or more | `about 1 h 5 min` |
103	
104	The estimate follows the format, **Speed:**, the size, the frame rate and the range.
105	
106	It's only an estimate. The figures behind it are the median of three measured exports at 1080p and at 4K, of real 4K camera footage on an idle Apple M2 Max. On 30-second exports at 2560 × 1440, which weren't part of those measurements, it came within 14 % of the real time. A slower Mac, a busy one or a heavy timeline takes longer.
107	
108	## The footnote
109	
110	The small line under the readout names what the file is made of. It lists these in order, leaving out whatever doesn't apply:
111	
112	1. The codec, such as `H264`, `AV1` or `PRORES422`.
113	2. The container, unless it's the same word as the codec, as in `GIF`.
114	3. The AV1 speed, such as `Balanced`.
115	4. `24-bit` for a 24-bit WAV or AIFF.
116	5. The number of stems, such as `3 stems`.
117	6. The video rate, when you've picked a Quality tier. AV1 and VP9 rates read `usually ≤ …`, because the rate is a [soft cap](/export/av1-and-vp9/#the-rate-as-a-soft-cap).
118	7. The audio rate, when you've picked a Quality tier, such as `192 kbps audio`.
119	8. The loudness target, such as `−14 LUFS`.
120	9. `alpha`, when the format keeps transparency.
121	
122	So a plain export reads `H264 · MP4`, an AV1 file `AV1 · MP4 · Balanced` or `AV1 · WEBM · Balanced`, and a transparent web movie `VP9 · WEBM · alpha`. With High quality and a loudness target at 1080p and 30 fps, an H.264 file reads `H264 · MP4 · 8.0 Mbps · 256 kbps audio · −14 LUFS`.
123	
124	## The remembered choice
125	
126	The sheet reopens on the last choices you exported with. Choosing **Export…** or **Add to Queue** records them, and **Cancel** doesn't. With nothing remembered, it opens on H.264 at the document's own size.
127	
128	The remembered choice belongs to the app, not the project, so every document's sheet opens on it.
129	
130	- Only what the format could use is remembered. After a WAV, for example, there's no size or frame rate to bring back. **Speed:**, **Bit depth:** and **Stems:** are the exception, and are remembered on every format.
131	- A remembered size row that the popup doesn't show falls back to a row with the same numbers, or else to the format's default.
132	- A remembered **In/out range** falls back to **Whole project** on a document with no range.
133	- **Dynamic Range:** isn't remembered. It opens on **HDR (HLG)** every time.
134	
135	To keep a set of choices under a name, save an [export preset](/export/presets/).
136	
137	## Export or Add to Queue
138	
139	The sheet ends in three buttons.
140	
141	| Button | What it does |
142	| --- | --- |
143	| **Cancel** | Closes the sheet. Nothing is written and nothing is remembered. |
144	| **Export…** | Opens a save panel, then writes the file behind a [progress sheet](/export/progress-and-report/). It doesn't join the queue and never waits for memory. |
145	| **Add to Queue** | Opens the same save panel, then puts the job in the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/). The job keeps the project as it is now, and you can go on editing. |
146	
147	**Export…** and **Add to Queue** are greyed out while the sheet can't work out a valid file, for example with an empty custom field, or when the file would have no length.
148	
149	The save panel suggests the project's name with the format's extension, such as `Board v1.2.mp4`. Its message says what's being written: "Export the timeline as a movie.", "Export the timeline as an animated GIF." or "Export the timeline's audio."
150	
151	## Good to know
152	
153	- An audio-only format on a timeline with no sound stops after the save panel with "There is nothing on the timeline to export — add a clip first."
154	- The readout accepts a custom size of a different shape from the canvas, but the movie formats that keep transparency stop on it after the save panel. See [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/).
155	
156	## With an agent
157	
158	`export` starts the job and returns at once, and `export_status` reports how it's going, with the sheet's time estimate as `estimated_seconds`. `cancel_export` stops it. Every agent export goes through the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/), never behind a progress sheet, and on an empty timeline `export` stops with an error instead of starting a job.
159	
160	`export` takes the sheet's choices but not **Frame rate:**, so it writes the document's rate, or GIF's and APNG's own. It can also set a ceiling for the master limiter other than the sheet's fixed one, and it replaces an existing file at its path. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).
161

221	
222	## Sound in each format
223	
224	Every file with sound is stereo at 48 kHz.
225	
226	| Sound | Formats |
227	| --- | --- |
228	| AAC | H.264, HEVC, HEVC with Alpha, HEVC 10-bit, AV1 (MP4) and M4A |
229	| Opus | AV1 (WebM), VP9 (WebM) and VP9 with Alpha (WebM) |
230	| 16-bit LPCM | ProRes 422 and ProRes 4444 |
231	| 16-bit or 24-bit LPCM | WAV and AIFF. See [Export bit depth](/export/bit-depth/). |
232	| None | GIF and APNG |

234	AAC and Opus run at 192 kbps unless a [Quality tier](/export/quality/) says otherwise.
235	
236	A file's sound is as long as the range it exports, including when a clip in it plays faster or slower. A project with no sound exports a movie with no sound track, in a WebM as in any other movie format.
237	
238	## Changing the format
239	
240	Changing the format rebuilds the **Size:** list and returns it to that format's default, because a GIF's default isn't an H.264's. Your frame rate, quality, loudness and range choices stay as they were, whether or not the new format can use them.
241	
242	Picking the format that's already chosen changes nothing, so a custom size you've typed survives it.
243	
244	## Software and hardware encoders
245	
246	AV1 and VP9 are encoded in software, by encoders built into Frame Job, so they take longer to export than the HEVC formats, which use the Mac's hardware encoder. The sheet [estimates the time](/export/export-sheet/#estimated-time) for AV1 and VP9, and AV1's [**Speed:** row](/export/encoder-speed/) trades time against file size.
247	
248	## No encoder
249	
250	A Mac with no encoder for a format reports it and leaves no file. The message names the format by its short name, for example: "This Mac cannot export with the “hevc_alpha” preset." Choose another format.
251	
252	## With an agent
253	
254	`export` names a format by its preset, such as `h264` or `vp9_alpha_webm`. [Presets](/mcp/export/#presets) lists all fifteen beside the names in the popup.

264	---
265	title: Export quality
266	description: Set how many bits an export spends on its picture and sound, from Format default to the four tiers.
267	---
268	
269	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
270	
271	The **Quality** popup sets the data rate of the picture and the sound. A higher rate gives a better picture and a larger file.
272	
273	<AtAGlance
274	  menu="File ▸ Export…"
275	  keys="⌘E"
276	  where="Export sheet ▸ Quality"
277	  tools="export"
278	/>
279	
280	## Choose a quality
281	
282	Open the export sheet and pick a row in **Quality**: **Format default**, **Low**, **Medium**, **High** or **Maximum**. Each tier's title shows the rate it would ask for at the size and frame rate now chosen, for example `High · 8.0 Mbps`.
283	
284	Once you pick a tier, the footnote shows the rates too, for example `H264 · MP4 · 8.0 Mbps · 256 kbps audio`. With **Format default** it shows no rates.
285	
286	## Format default
287	
288	The default row. Frame Job works the rate out from the frame's size and rate:
289	
290	| Format | At 1080p, 30 fps | Bits per pixel per frame |
291	| --- | --- | --- |
292	| H.264 | About 8.7 Mbps | 0.14 |
293	| HEVC, HEVC with Alpha, HEVC 10-bit | About 4.4 Mbps | 0.07 |
294	| AV1, VP9 | A [cap](#rates-on-av1-and-vp9) of about 4.4 Mbps | 0.07 |
295	
296	The rate rises in step with the frame's area and the frame rate, and it's held between 1 and 200 Mbps. So H.264 at 1080p is about 8.7 Mbps at 30 fps, a little above **High**, and about 17.4 Mbps at 60 fps, where **High** is 12.0 Mbps.
297	
298	The sound is 192 kbps AAC, or 192 kbps Opus in the WebM formats.
299	
300	## The four tiers
301	
302	Each tier sets the rate from the frame's size, so a tier means the same picture quality at every size. These are the H.264 rates at 30 fps or less:
303	
304	| Tier | Bits per pixel per frame | 720p | 1080p | 4K | Sound |
305	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
306	| **Low** | 0.064 | 1.8 Mbps | 4.0 Mbps | 15.9 Mbps | 128 kbps |
307	| **Medium** | 0.096 | 2.7 Mbps | 6.0 Mbps | 23.9 Mbps | 192 kbps |
308	| **High** | 0.129 | 3.6 Mbps | 8.0 Mbps | 32.1 Mbps | 256 kbps |
309	| **Maximum** | 0.193 | 5.3 Mbps | 12.0 Mbps | 48.0 Mbps | 320 kbps |
310	
311	A [preset](/export/presets/) stores the tier, not the number, so "High" works out the right rate on any document.
312	
313	## How the rate scales
314	
315	- **Frame size.** The rate scales with the frame's area, using the size you chose rather than the canvas's.
316	- **Frame rate.** Above 30.5 fps the rate is 1.5 times higher, so 50 and 60 fps are raised and 29.97 and 30 fps aren't. **High** at 1080p and 60 fps is 12.0 Mbps in H.264.
317	- **Codec.** HEVC reaches the same picture at roughly 60 % of H.264's rate, so the HEVC formats ask for 60 % of it, and AV1 and VP9 use the same figure. **High** at 1080p is 4.8 Mbps in HEVC.
318	- **Rounding.** A rate is rounded to the nearest 100 kbps, and it never goes below 100 kbps.
319	
320	## Rates on AV1 and VP9
321	
322	On AV1 and VP9 the rate is a soft cap. The encoder works to a constant quality chosen to match HEVC at that rate, so the file usually stays under it. Very detailed footage can go over, by up to about 1.25 times the rate on AV1 and about 1.15 times on VP9.
323	
324	The tier titles and the footnote say so, for example `High · usually ≤ 4.8 Mbps`. AV1's cap stops at 100 Mbps, the most its encoder takes.
325	
326	On VP9 with Alpha (WebM) the rate covers the picture alone. The transparency is a second stream on top of it, so the file is larger than the rate says. See [AV1 and VP9](/export/av1-and-vp9/).
327	
328	## Sound rates
329	
330	A tier sets the sound rate as well as the video rate.
331	
332	| Row | Sound |
333	| --- | --- |
334	| **Format default** | 192 kbps |
335	| **Low** | 128 kbps |
336	| **Medium** | 192 kbps |
337	| **High** | 256 kbps |
338	| **Maximum** | 320 kbps |
339	
340	The H.264, HEVC and AV1 (MP4) formats use these as AAC rates. The WebM formats ask the same rates of their Opus sound, rounded to the nearest rate the Opus encoder offers.
341	
342	**Audio only (M4A)** has no picture, so a tier sets its AAC rate alone, and its titles read `High · 256 kbps`.
343	
344	## When Quality greys out
345	
346	**Quality** is greyed out for ProRes 422, ProRes 4444, WAV, AIFF, Animated GIF and Animated PNG, where the format fixes the rate. ProRes takes its rate from its profile and carries uncompressed sound, WAV and AIFF are uncompressed, and GIF and APNG have no rate at all.
347	
348	## With an agent
349	
350	An agent doesn't pick a tier. It passes `video_bitrate` and `audio_bitrate` to `export` in bits per second, so 8000000 is 8 Mbps, and leaving them out gives **Format default**. ProRes, GIF and APNG ignore `video_bitrate`, and ProRes, WAV and AIFF ignore `audio_bitrate`. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/#exact-bitrates).

403	## Type a custom size
404	
405	<Steps>
406	
407	1. Choose **Custom…** in **Size**. The two fields on the row below become editable, holding the size that was chosen a moment before.
408	
409	2. Type a width and a height, from 16 to 8192 pixels each.

415	A number outside the range stays in the field, and **Export…** beeps until you fix it. With a field empty, **Export…** and **Add to Queue** are greyed out and the readout says "Type a width and a height, or pick a size from the list."
416	
417	## Sizes that repeat
418	
419	A row with the same numbers as an earlier row is hidden, so one size shows once, under the name that says more. A 1920 × 1080 document shows **Document size** and no separate **1080p**.
420	
421	A saved preset that names a hidden row still works. It lands on the row showing the same numbers.
422	
423	## Export larger than the document
424	
425	The list offers sizes larger than the document, so a 720p recording can go out at 4K for a platform that picks its bit rate by resolution.
426	
427	A movie is scaled up to the size you choose. The picture is drawn at the canvas size first, so a larger frame holds more pixels but no more detail.
428	
429	GIF and APNG are never enlarged. They fit the picture inside the size you choose, as [Good to know](#good-to-know) explains.
430	
431	## Odd widths and heights
432	
433	H.264, HEVC, HEVC with Alpha, HEVC 10-bit, both AV1 formats, both VP9 formats and ProRes 422 need even dimensions. On these formats an odd width or height is written one pixel smaller, and the readout shows the size the file will really have. This applies to a custom size as well as to the canvas.
434	
435	ProRes 4444, GIF and APNG keep an odd edge.
436	
437	## A different shape from the canvas
438	
439	A movie is written at exactly the size you choose. What happens to the picture depends on how close that size is to the canvas's shape:
440	
441	- **Within a pixel of the canvas's shape**, the picture fills the frame edge to edge, with no black line along an edge.
442	- **Any other shape** is letterboxed with black.
443	
444	Only **Custom…** can give you a different shape, because every row in the list has the canvas's shape.
445	
446	ProRes 4444, HEVC with Alpha and VP9 with Alpha (WebM) don't letterbox, because the padding would destroy the alpha channel. The sheet lets you choose the size, but Frame Job won't write the file: the export stops with a message naming the canvas and the size you asked for. Use a size with the canvas's proportions instead. An odd size typed in those proportions is fine. See [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/).
447	
448	## Good to know
449	
450	- GIF and APNG fit the picture inside the size you choose, keeping its shape and never enlarging it, so they have no letterbox. Their rows show the fitted numbers: a 1080 × 1920 project's **GIF default** is 152 × 270. See [Animated GIF and PNG](/export/gif-and-apng/).
451	- **Size** is greyed out for the [audio-only formats](/export/audio-only/).
452	- A preset stores the row you chose rather than its numbers, so "4K" comes out at the right 4K size for each document. See [Export presets](/export/presets/).
453	
454	## With an agent
455	
456	An agent passes `size` to `export`: `document`, the default, then `2160p`, `1440p`, `1080p`, `720p`, `preset` for the GIF and APNG default, or `[width, height]` for a custom size. A custom size outside 16 to 8192 pixels is an error. Every named size works on every document, including one the sheet hides as a repeat. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/#size).
457

464	=================== frame-rate
465	---
466	title: Export frame rate
467	description: Export at the project's own frame rate, or at a fixed rate from 23.976 to 60 fps.
468	---
469	
470	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
471	
472	The **Frame rate** popup sets how many frames a second the exported file has, without changing the project.
473	
474	<AtAGlance
475	  menu="File ▸ Export…"
476	  keys="⌘E"
477	  where="Export sheet ▸ Frame rate"
478	  tools="export"
479	/>
480	
481	## Choose a frame rate
482	
483	Open the export sheet and pick a row in **Frame rate**. The readout under the controls shows the rate the file will have.
484	
485	**Project rate** is the default. It's the document's [frame rate](/projects/frame-rate/), or the format's own rate for Animated GIF (12.5 fps) and Animated PNG (25 fps).
486	
487	The fixed rows, in the popup's order, are **24 fps**, **23.976 fps**, **25 fps**, **30 fps**, **29.97 fps**, **50 fps** and **60 fps**.
488	
489	Frame Job draws the same timeline at the new rate, so the export runs for the same length of time and only the number of frames changes.
490	
491	## What else the rate changes
492	
493	- **The range.** The start and length of the export are snapped to the export's frame grid, which moves each by less than a frame. See [Export a range](/export/range/).
494	- **The bit rate.** On **Format default** the video rate rises in step with the frame rate. The [Quality](/export/quality/) tiers rise by half above 30.5 fps, and each tier's title shows the new number.
495	- **The time an AV1 or VP9 export takes.** The estimate in the readout counts frames, so it follows the rate.
496	
497	## Good to know
498	
499	- **Frame rate** is greyed out for the [audio-only formats](/export/audio-only/), which have no frames.
500	- A fixed rate you export with is remembered with the rest of the sheet, and every document's sheet opens on it. Check it before you export a project with a different rate. Choose **Project rate** to go back. See [The export sheet](/export/export-sheet/).
501	- A preset stores the rate you chose. **Project rate** stays **Project rate**, so it follows each document.
502	
503	## With an agent
504	
505	An agent can't set the frame rate. Its `export` uses the document's rate, or the format's own rate for GIF and APNG. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).
506

520	
521	The **Bit depth** row sets how finely a WAV or AIFF file records each sample of the sound. It's about sound only. The depth of the picture comes from the format you choose, and is on [Precision and bit depth](/hdr/precision/).
522	
523	<AtAGlance
524	  menu="File ▸ Export…"
525	  keys="⌘E"
526	  where="Export sheet ▸ Bit depth"
527	  tools="export"
528	/>
529	
530	## Choose a bit depth
531	
532	In the export sheet, choose **Audio only (WAV)** or **Audio only (AIFF)** in **Format**, then pick a row in **Bit depth**, which sits under **Quality**.
533	
534	| Row | What it's for |
535	| --- | --- |
536	| **16-bit** | The default. About 11.5 MB a minute. |
537	| **24-bit** | Keeps detail 16-bit can't. It matters most for a quiet recording you're going to raise or process later. About 17.3 MB a minute. |
538	
539	A 24-bit file shows `24-bit` in the footnote, for example `LPCM · WAV · 24-bit`.
540	
541	Both depths are rounded once from the [float mix](/export/audio-only/#the-48-khz-stereo-master), to the nearest value, and neither is dithered.
542

544	
545	- On every other format **Bit depth** is greyed out and keeps your last choice.
546	- ProRes sound stays 16-bit, and AAC and Opus sound is encoded from 16-bit samples.
547	- The choice is remembered with the rest of the sheet and stored in [presets](/export/presets/).
548	
549	## With an agent
550

558	=================== encoder-speed
559	---
560	title: Encoder speed
561	description: Choose how long the AV1 encoder works on each frame, trading export time against file size.
562	---
563	
564	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
565	
566	The **Speed** row sets how long the AV1 encoder works on each frame. A longer time gives a smaller file, so it's a choice between waiting less and sending less.
567	
568	<AtAGlance
569	  menu="File ▸ Export…"
570	  keys="⌘E"
571	  where="Export sheet ▸ Speed"
572	  tools="export"
573	/>
574	
575	## Choose a speed
576	
577	In the export sheet, choose **AV1 (MP4)** or **AV1 (WebM)** in **Format**, then pick a row in **Speed**. The row sits under **Format**, or under **Dynamic Range** in an HDR project.
578	
579	| Speed | What it does | SVT-AV1 preset |
580	| --- | --- | --- |
581	| **Faster** | The quickest export and the largest file. | 8 |
582	| **Balanced** | The default. | 6 |
583	| **Smaller file** | The slowest export and the smallest file. | 4 |
584	
585	The footnote names your choice, for example `AV1 · MP4 · Balanced`, and the estimate in the readout follows it, for example `Estimated time: about 25 s`. The estimate is only a guide. Its figures come from an idle Apple M2 Max, so a slower or busy Mac, or a heavy timeline, takes longer.
586	
587	The rate from [Quality](/export/quality/) is the cap at every speed, and each speed is tuned to match HEVC's picture at that rate. So Speed moves the time and the file size, not the quality you asked for.
588	
589	## What each speed costs
590	
591	Measured on 10 seconds of 4K camera footage on an Apple M2 Max, exported as AV1 (MP4):
592	
593	| Speed | Time at 4K | File at 4K | Time at 1080p | File at 1080p |
594	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
595	| **Faster** | 7.1 s | 27 % larger | 2.4 s | 4 % larger |
596	| **Balanced** | 14.0 s | The baseline | 4.2 s | The baseline |
597	| **Smaller file** | 19.9 s | 12 % smaller | 5.8 s | 5 % smaller |
598	
599	The file size **Faster** adds is much greater at 4K than at 1080p, where it costs little.
600	
601	Speed changes the memory an export uses too. **Faster** measured about 1.3 GB at 1080p and 4.6 GB at 4K, **Balanced** about 2.2 GB and 7.5 GB, and **Smaller file** about 2.4 GB and 8.1 GB. AV1 and VP9 exports share a quarter of the Mac's memory, and a job that would go over it [waits for memory](/export/export-queue/#the-encoder-memory-wait) in the Export Queue.
602	
603	## Good to know
604	
605	- On every other format **Speed** is greyed out and keeps your last choice. That includes VP9 (WebM) and VP9 with Alpha (WebM), because VP9 has one speed.
606	- The choice is remembered with the rest of the sheet and stored in [presets](/export/presets/).
607	
608	## With an agent
609	
610	An agent passes `encoder_speed` to `export`, as `faster`, `balanced` or `smaller`. `balanced` is the default. It works on `av1` and `av1_webm` only, and any other format returns an error. The finished export's result names the speed used. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/#encoder-speed).
611	
612	## Related

614	- [AV1 and VP9](/export/av1-and-vp9/)
615	- [Export quality](/export/quality/)
616	- [The Export Queue](/export/export-queue/)
617	=================== h264-and-hevc
618	---
619	title: "H.264 and HEVC"
620	description: "Know what the H.264, HEVC, HEVC 10-bit and HEVC with Alpha formats write, and which one suits your delivery file."
621	---
622	
623	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
624	
625	These four formats are for delivery. H.264 is the file everything takes, HEVC is smaller, HEVC 10-bit keeps a deep source's gradients, and HEVC with Alpha keeps a transparent canvas.
626	
627	<AtAGlance
628	  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
629	  tools="export"
630	/>
631	
632	| Format | File | Picture | Keeps transparency | In an HDR project | Rate at 1080p, 30 fps with Format default |
633	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
634	| [H.264 (MP4)](#h264-mp4) | `.mp4` | 8-bit | No | Writes the SDR version | About 8.7 Mbps |
635	| [HEVC (MP4)](#hevc-mp4) | `.mp4` | 8-bit | No | Writes the SDR version | About 4.4 Mbps |
636	| [HEVC 10-bit (MP4)](#hevc-10-bit-mp4) | `.mp4` | 10-bit | No | Writes HDR | About 4.4 Mbps |
637	| [HEVC with Alpha (MOV)](#hevc-with-alpha-mov) | `.mov` | 8-bit | Yes | Writes the SDR version | About 4.4 Mbps |
638	
639	All four share these:
640	
641	- A keyframe at least every 2 seconds, so the file scrubs and re-cuts well.
642	- AAC sound, stereo at 48 kHz, at 192 kbps unless a [Quality tier](/export/quality/) says otherwise.
643	- Even dimensions. An odd width or height is written one pixel smaller. See [Export size](/export/size/).
644	- [Chapters](/export/chapters/) from your chapter markers.
645	- [Fast start](#fast-start) on the three MP4s.
646	
647	## H.264 (MP4)
648	
649	This is the default, the first row of the **Format:** popup, so <kbd>⌘E</kbd> writes it unless you've chosen otherwise. Every player and upload form takes it.
650	
651	It writes 8-bit video in the High profile, with the level chosen automatically. With **Format default**, the rate follows the frame at 0.14 bits per pixel per frame, held between 1 and 200 Mbps.
652	
653	H.264 has no alpha channel, so a transparent canvas is flattened onto black.
654	
655	## HEVC (MP4)
656	
657	HEVC gives you the same picture in about half the rate of H.264, though not everything accepts it yet. It uses the Mac's hardware encoder.
658	
659	It writes 8-bit video in the Main profile, even from a 10-bit source. With **Format default**, the rate is 0.07 bits per pixel per frame, held between 1 and 200 Mbps. The Quality tiers ask for 60 % of H.264's rate.
660	
661	## HEVC 10-bit (MP4)
662	
663	HEVC 10-bit writes HEVC's Main 10 profile from the 16-bit frames Frame Job draws, so a 10-bit source keeps its gradients in a delivery file. Its rates are HEVC's.
664	
665	It's one of the six formats that can carry HDR. In an HLG project it writes HLG unless you change **Dynamic Range:**, and no Dolby Vision is added to the file. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).
666	
667	## HEVC with Alpha (MOV)
668	
669	This is a small delivery movie that keeps a transparent canvas, for laying over another background. It's the transparent movie for Safari. For a web page in Chrome or Firefox, see [VP9 with Alpha (WebM)](/export/av1-and-vp9/#vp9-with-alpha-webm), and for a master, [ProRes 4444 (MOV)](/export/prores/#prores-4444-mov).
670	
671	- It's a `.mov` because this codec can't be written into an `.mp4`.
672	- The picture and its alpha are both 8-bit, and the colour is straight, not multiplied by the transparency. Transparent pixels beside the picture take its colour, so compression doesn't darken the edges.
673	- It takes HEVC's rates and Quality tiers, and the [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`.
674	- [Fast start](#fast-start) is off.
675	
676	Every row in the **Size:** popup has the canvas's shape, so those are all fine. A **Custom…** size of a different shape won't export, because padding it would lose the alpha. After the save panel the export stops with a message naming the canvas's size. A size within a pixel of the canvas's shape, or in the same proportions at any scale, is fine.
677	
678	## Fast start
679	
680	MP4 and M4A files are written with their index at the front, so a player can start before the whole file has downloaded. There's no control for this in the sheet.
681	
682	Fast start is on for MP4 and M4A, and off for MOV, WAV, AIFF, GIF and APNG. A WebM's index is at the front anyway.
683	
684	## Good to know
685	
686	H.264, HEVC and HEVC with Alpha are all 8-bit, so in an HDR project they write the project's SDR version and **Dynamic Range:** stays greyed out on **SDR version**. To deliver HDR in this family, use HEVC 10-bit.
687	
688	## With an agent
689	
690	`export` names these formats `h264`, `hevc`, `hevc_10bit` and `hevc_alpha`. It sets rates as numbers rather than tiers. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/#exact-bitrates).
691	
692	## Related
693	
694	- [Choose a format](/export/formats/)
695	- [Export quality](/export/quality/)
696	- [AV1 and VP9](/export/av1-and-vp9/)
697	- [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/)
698	- [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/)
699	=================== prores
700	---
701	title: "ProRes"
702	description: "Export a ProRes 422 or ProRes 4444 master for another application, and see what each one keeps."
703	---
704	
705	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
706	
707	ProRes files are masters: their next reader is another application, not a viewer. ProRes 422 is the one to reach for first. ProRes 4444 is larger, and you choose it when you need the alpha channel.
708	
709	<AtAGlance
710	  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
711	  tools="export"
712	/>
713	
714	| | ProRes 422 (MOV) | ProRes 4444 (MOV) |
715	| --- | --- | --- |
716	| Picture | 10-bit | 12-bit |
717	| Keeps transparency | No | Yes |
718	| Odd width or height | Written one pixel smaller | Kept |
719	| A custom size of a different shape | Letterboxed with black | Won't export |
720	
721	Both are `.mov` files with these in common:
722	
723	- The data rate is fixed by the profile, so **Quality:** is greyed out.
724	- The sound is 16-bit, 48 kHz stereo LPCM. **Bit depth:** is greyed out, because 24-bit is for WAV and AIFF.
725	- Both can carry HDR. In an HLG project they write HLG unless you change **Dynamic Range:**. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).
726	- [Chapters](/export/chapters/) are written.
727	- [Fast start](/export/h264-and-hevc/#fast-start) is off, because an editing master has no need of it.
728	
729	## ProRes 422 (MOV)
730	
731	Use this as an editing master for another application. It keeps 10 bits of the 16-bit frames Frame Job draws.
732	
733	ProRes 422 has no alpha channel, so a transparent canvas is flattened onto black.
734	
735	## ProRes 4444 (MOV)
736	
737	Use this for a title, a lower third or anything else another application will composite over its own footage. It keeps 12 bits and the alpha channel, and the [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`. The colour is straight, not multiplied by the transparency, so a re-imported file composites to the right colour.
738	
739	It's the only movie format that keeps an odd width or height.
740	
741	A **Custom…** size of a different shape from the canvas won't export, because padding would lose the alpha. After the save panel the export stops with a message naming the canvas's size. Every row in the **Size:** popup has the canvas's shape, and any custom size in the same proportions is fine.
742	
743	## With an agent
744	
745	`export` names these formats `prores_422` and `prores_4444`. Both ignore `video_bitrate` and `audio_bitrate`, because the profile sets the rate and the sound is uncompressed. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/#exact-bitrates).
746	
747	## Related

753	=================== av1-and-vp9
754	---
755	title: "AV1 and VP9"
756	description: "Export delivery files and web movies with Frame Job's built-in AV1 and VP9 encoders, and know how their rates, time and memory behave."
757	---
758	
759	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
760	
761	AV1 and VP9 aim to match or beat HEVC's picture at the same rate, and their WebM formats are for the web. Frame Job has their encoders built in, SVT-AV1 4.2.0 and libvpx 1.17.0. They run in software, so an export takes longer than HEVC's.
762	
763	<AtAGlance
764	  where={['Export sheet ▸ Format', 'Export sheet ▸ Speed (AV1 only)']}
765	  tools="export"
766	/>
767	
768	| Format | File | Sound | Picture | Keeps transparency | Can carry HDR | **Speed:** |
769	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
770	| [AV1 (MP4)](#av1-mp4) | `.mp4` | AAC | 10-bit | No | Yes | Yes |
771	| [AV1 (WebM)](#av1-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 10-bit | No | Yes | Yes |
772	| [VP9 (WebM)](#vp9-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit, or 10-bit with HDR | No | Yes | Greyed out |
773	| [VP9 with Alpha (WebM)](#vp9-with-alpha-webm) | `.webm` | Opus | 8-bit | Yes | No | Greyed out |
774	
775	All four write a keyframe at least every 2 seconds and need even dimensions, so an odd width or height is written one pixel smaller. All four write [chapters](/export/chapters/). The sheet [estimates the time](/export/export-sheet/#estimated-time) before you start.
776	
777	## AV1 (MP4)
778	
779	This is AV1 video and AAC sound in an MP4, for delivery. It's always 10-bit.
780	
781	**Speed:** offers **Faster**, **Balanced** and **Smaller file**, with **Balanced** the default. See [Encoder speed](/export/encoder-speed/). Slower settings take longer and write a smaller file.
782	
783	It encodes at a constant quality matched to HEVC, with the rate as a [soft cap](#the-rate-as-a-soft-cap). It's one of the six formats that can carry HDR. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).
784	
785	An M1 or M2 Mac can't [play the file back](#playback-on-m1-and-m2-macs).
786	
787	## AV1 (WebM)
788	
789	The same AV1 picture in a WebM file, for the web. It has the same encoder, speeds, soft cap and HDR as AV1 (MP4). Only the container and the sound differ.
790	
791	The sound is Opus, 48 kHz stereo, at 192 kbps unless a [Quality tier](/export/quality/) says otherwise, and it snaps to the nearest rate the encoder offers. A project with no sound exports a WebM with no sound track.
792	
793	## VP9 (WebM)
794	
795	VP9 in a WebM file with Opus sound, for the web. It has one speed, so **Speed:** is greyed out. For the same picture the file is larger than AV1's. Its rate is a [soft cap](#the-rate-as-a-soft-cap) too.
796	
797	An SDR picture is 8-bit, in VP9's Profile 0. HDR is 10-bit, in Profile 2. VP9 can't name HLG or PQ itself, so the WebM file tells the player which one it is. See [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).
798	
799	## VP9 with Alpha (WebM)
800	
801	VP9 (WebM) that keeps a transparent canvas, for a title or lower third a web page plays over its own background in Chrome or Firefox. Safari's transparent movie is [HEVC with Alpha (MOV)](/export/h264-and-hevc/#hevc-with-alpha-mov).
802	
803	- The picture is 8-bit, with the transparency as a second stream beside it. The [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`.
804	- It's SDR only, so an HDR project writes its SDR version, and **Dynamic Range:** stays greyed out on **SDR version**.
805	- The sound is Opus, as in VP9 (WebM).
806	- A **Custom…** size of a different shape from the canvas won't export, because padding would lose the alpha. After the save panel the export stops with a message naming the canvas's size. Every row in the **Size:** popup is fine.
807	- Imported back into Frame Job it shows opaque, because the transparency isn't read. For a transparent clip to bring back in, export ProRes 4444 or HEVC with Alpha.
808	
809	## The rate as a soft cap
810	
811	On AV1 and VP9 the video rate isn't a target. They encode at a constant quality chosen to match or beat HEVC at that rate, and the file usually stays under it. That's why the Quality tiers and the footnote read `usually ≤ …`.
812	
813	With **Format default** the cap is HEVC's rate. With a tier it's 60 % of the H.264 rate, as for HEVC. See [Export quality](/export/quality/). An AV1 rate is held at 100 Mbps at most. In an HDR export, VP9 matches HEVC 10-bit at that rate.
814	
815	You can't know the file size in advance. Simple footage comes out much smaller than the rate. Very detailed footage can go over it, by up to about 1.25 times the rate as measured on AV1 and about 1.15 times on VP9.
816	
817	On VP9 with Alpha the rate is the picture's alone. The transparency is a second stream at a fixed quality on top of it, so the file is larger than the rate says. Measured on a moving soft-edged shape, the transparency added this much to the video's size:
818	
819	| Size | Added to the video |
820	| --- | --- |
821	| 1080p | About 6–15 % |
822	| 720p | About 9–21 % |
823	| 640 × 360 | About 21–39 % |
824	
825	The higher figure in each row is at the **Low** tier.
826	
827	## Memory and the queue
828	
829	AV1 and VP9 need a lot of memory. A job in the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) waits if starting it would take the AV1 and VP9 exports running at that moment past a quarter of the Mac's memory. Its row says why, for example "Waiting for memory: AV1 and VP9 exports running now hold about 6.0 GB of the 8.0 GB this Mac allows them, and this one needs about 3.0 GB." A later job may run first meanwhile.
830	
831	A job always starts when no other AV1 or VP9 export is running. **Export…** never waits, so starting several at once behind their progress sheets can go past that quarter. The memory each job needs is a measured figure, not a guarantee.
832	
833	## Playback on M1 and M2 Macs
834	
835	M1 and M2 Macs have no AV1 decoder, so neither Frame Job nor QuickTime can play an AV1 file there, MP4 or WebM, and Frame Job can't re-import one. An import stops with a message saying the file needs an M3 or later Mac. The Mac can still export one.
836	
837	A VP9 (WebM) file re-imports on any Apple silicon Mac.
838	
839	## With an agent
840	
841	`export` names these formats `av1`, `av1_webm`, `vp9_webm` and `vp9_alpha_webm`. `video_bitrate` is the same soft cap, on the picture's stream alone for `vp9_alpha_webm`, and `encoder_speed` sets AV1's speed. `export_status` gives the time estimate as `estimated_seconds`. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/#exact-bitrates).
842

848	- [The Export Queue](/export/export-queue/)
849	=================== gif-and-apng
850	---
851	title: "Animated GIF and PNG"
852	description: "Export a short silent loop as an Animated GIF or Animated PNG, and keep it inside the size and the 600-frame limit."
853	---
854	
855	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
856	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
857	
858	GIF and APNG are for short silent loops you can send or drop into a page. Each stores every frame as a whole picture, so a long or large one quickly becomes a file nobody can send. That's why both start small and hold at most 600 frames.
859	
860	<AtAGlance
861	  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
862	  tools="export"
863	/>
864	
865	## Export a loop
866	
867	<Steps>
868	
869	1. Set an [in/out range](/timeline/in-out-range/) around the moment you want.
870	
871	2. Press <kbd>⌘E</kbd>, and choose **Animated GIF** or **Animated PNG** from **Format:**.
872	
873	3. Set **Range:** to **In/out range**.
874	
875	4. Check the readout, which shows the size and the frame count, such as `· 360 frames, no audio`.
876	
877	5. Choose **Export…**.
878	
879	</Steps>
880	
881	## Animated GIF
882	
883	A GIF is a short, silent `.gif` that loops forever. It starts at 480 × 270 and 12.5 fps, and you can still change the size and the rate.
884	
885	The 12.5 is deliberate. A GIF stores each frame's delay in hundredths of a second, so only rates that divide 100 play back exactly. 25 and 50 fps from the **Frame rate:** popup do too, and any other rate lands wherever the format's rounding puts it.
886	
887	A GIF has a palette of 256 colours. It can show a pixel as fully transparent but has no partial transparency, so soft edges go hard, and it isn't one of the [formats that keep transparency](/export/transparency/).
888	
889	## Animated PNG
890	
891	An APNG is a lossless, silent, true-colour `.png` that loops forever. It starts at 960 × 540 and 25 fps, and you can still change the size and the rate.
892	
893	It keeps real transparency, so a pixel can be any fraction of opaque, and the [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`. It's written at 8 bits a component and labelled BT.709.
894	
895	A viewer that knows nothing of APNG shows the first frame.
896	
897	## The 600-frame limit
898	
899	An animated GIF or APNG holds at most 600 frames. That's 48 seconds at GIF's 12.5 fps, or 24 seconds at APNG's 25 fps. The readout shows the count while you're choosing, but the sheet doesn't stop you. Once you've picked where to save, a longer export stops before it writes anything:
900	
901	> An animated GIF is limited to 600 frames and this range is 720. Shorten the range, or lower the export frame rate.
902	
903	For GIF the way out is a shorter range, because every fixed rate in the **Frame rate:** popup is higher than 12.5 fps. An APNG can go down to 24 or 23.976 fps, which gains you about a second.
904	
905	## Fitting inside the size
906	
907	The **Size:** popup lists **GIF default** or **APNG default** first, and it's the default for those two formats and no others. **GIF default** is 480 × 270 and **APNG default** is 960 × 540, each fitted to the canvas's shape.
908	
909	Every row, and a **Custom…** size, is a box the picture fits inside. It keeps its shape and is never enlarged, and nothing is letterboxed. The rows show the size the file will have. A 1080 × 1920 project's GIF default is 152 × 270.
910	
911	Because the picture is never enlarged, rows bigger than the canvas come out as the canvas's own size, and the popup hides rows that repeat an earlier row's numbers. An odd width or height is kept.
912	
913	## Good to know
914	
915	- **Quality:** and **Loudness:** are greyed out, and so are **Bit depth:** and **Stems:**. Neither format has a bit rate or any sound.
916	- **Burn in timecode** still works.
917	- Neither format has [chapters](/export/chapters/).
918	- Both write the SDR version in an HDR project.
919	
920	## With an agent
921	
922	`export` names these formats `gif` and `apng`. Their default rows are `size: "preset"`, which no other format takes. There's no frame-rate argument, so an agent's GIF is always 12.5 fps and its APNG 25 fps. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/#size).
923	
924	## Related
925	
926	- [Choose a format](/export/formats/)
927	- [Export a range](/export/range/)
928	- [Export size](/export/size/)
929	- [Export frame rate](/export/frame-rate/)
930	=================== transparency
931	---
932	title: "Transparent exports"
933	description: "Export a title or overlay with a transparent background, and choose the format that keeps it for the place it's going."
934	---
935	
936	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
937	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
938	
939	A transparent canvas lets you export a title, a lower third or an overlay that sits on top of something else. Only four formats keep the transparency, so the format is the choice that matters.
940	
941	<AtAGlance
942	  where={['Document tab ▸ Appearance ▸ Background', 'Export sheet ▸ Format']}
943	  tools={['set_canvas', 'export']}
944	/>
945	
946	## Export with transparency
947	
948	<Steps>
949	
950	1. [Make the canvas background transparent](/projects/background-and-timecode/#make-the-background-transparent) in the Document tab.
951	
952	2. Open the [export sheet](/export/export-sheet/) and pick a format that keeps transparency. The sheet's [footnote](/export/export-sheet/#the-footnote) ends in `alpha`, for example `VP9 · WEBM · alpha`.
953	
954	3. Choose **Export…** or **Add to Queue**.
955	
956	</Steps>
957	
958	## Which formats keep transparency
959	
960	A transparent canvas stays transparent in four formats:
961	
962	- **ProRes 4444 (MOV)**
963	- **HEVC with Alpha (MOV)**
964	- **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)**
965	- **Animated PNG**
966	
967	Every other format draws the picture onto black. **Animated GIF** isn't one of the four either: a GIF can show a pixel as fully transparent, but it has no alpha channel, so nothing partly transparent survives it.
968	
969	For a single frame, [Save Frame](/export/save-frame/#png-jpeg-or-heic) keeps transparency in PNG and HEIC, and JPEG flattens onto black.
970	
971	## The Transparency note
972	
973	While the canvas background isn't fully opaque, the **Appearance** section of the [Document tab](/projects/document-tab/) says how many formats will keep it: "Transparent — kept by 4 export formats."
974	
975	If only one or two formats could keep it, the note names them instead of counting. A document with no length can read "Transparent — needs an alpha format."
976	
977	## Which transparent movie to send
978	
979	| Send | For | Good to know |
980	| --- | --- | --- |
981	| **VP9 with Alpha (WebM)** | The web, in a page's `<video>` in Chrome and Firefox | Whether Safari shows its transparency hasn't been confirmed, so send Safari HEVC with Alpha. |
982	| **HEVC with Alpha (MOV)** | Safari, QuickTime and Apple's apps | The delivery file: lossy, 8-bit and smaller than ProRes 4444. |
983	| **ProRes 4444 (MOV)** | Another editor | The master. |
984	
985	VP9 with Alpha shows its transparency only in a player that decodes VP9 with the libvpx decoder. Others, ffmpeg's default decoder among them, show the picture opaque.
986	
987	To bring a transparent clip back into Frame Job, export ProRes 4444 or HEVC with Alpha. A VP9 with Alpha file keeps its picture when you import it but loses its transparency, showing black where it was transparent.
988	
989	## Straight alpha
990	
991	The colour in all three transparent movies is straight, not multiplied by the transparency, so a re-imported ProRes 4444 or HEVC with Alpha file composites to the right colour. If another app asks how a file's transparency is stored, choose straight.
992	
993	Frame Job also fills the transparent pixels around the picture, up to 4 pixels out, with the colour of the edge beside them. Without that, a codec that averages colour across pixels would darken the edge. This is automatic, and there's nothing to set.
994	
995	## The same-shape rule
996	
997	ProRes 4444, HEVC with Alpha and VP9 with Alpha won't write a frame of a different shape from the canvas. Fitting the picture into another shape would pad it, and the padding destroys the alpha channel.
998	
999	Every row in the [**Size:** popup](/export/size/) has the canvas's shape, so this only happens with a **Custom…** size. Scaling is fine, larger or smaller, as long as the proportions hold, and a size within a pixel of the canvas's shape is written.
1000	
1001	After the save panel, the export stops with a message naming both sizes: "An export that keeps transparency has to have the canvas's own shape. This canvas is 1920 × 1080 and 1000 × 1000 is a different shape, so the picture would be padded and the padding loses the alpha channel. Export at 1920 × 1080, at one of the sizes in the popup, or at any size with the same proportions."
1002	
1003	## Good to know
1004	
1005	HEVC with Alpha, VP9 with Alpha and Animated PNG are 8-bit. In an [HDR project](/hdr/export-hdr/) they write the SDR version, so use ProRes 4444 to keep both HDR and transparency.
1006

1	=================== audio-only
2	---
3	title: Audio-only exports
4	description: Export the timeline's sound with no picture, as a compressed M4A or an uncompressed WAV or AIFF.
5	---
6	
7	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
8	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
9	
10	Frame Job can write the timeline's sound with no picture: an M4A to send to someone, or a WAV or AIFF to hand to a mastering engineer, a DAW or a podcast editor.
11	
12	<AtAGlance
13	  menu="File ▸ Export…"
14	  keys="⌘E"
15	  where="Export sheet ▸ Format"
16	  tools="export"
17	/>
18	
19	## Export the sound
20	
21	<Steps>
22	
23	1. Choose **File ▸ Export…** or press <kbd>⌘E</kbd>.
24	
25	2. In **Format**, choose **Audio only (M4A)**, **Audio only (WAV)** or **Audio only (AIFF)**.
26	
27	3. Set the [controls that apply](#which-controls-apply). The [readout](/export/export-sheet/#the-readout-line) under the controls shows the length in milliseconds rather than frames, for example `Audio only · 00:01:12.200`.
28	
29	4. Choose **Export…**, or **Add to Queue** to keep editing while it's written, then name the file.
30	
31	</Steps>
32	
33	## Audio only (M4A)
34	
35	An `.m4a` file holding AAC sound, 48 kHz stereo. This is the one to send to someone, because it's by far the smallest.
36	
37	The sound is 192 kbps unless you pick a tier in [Quality](/export/quality/): **Low** is 128 kbps, **Medium** 192, **High** 256 and **Maximum** 320. The footnote reads `AAC · M4A`, with the rate added when you pick a tier.
38	
39	Chapter markers are written into the file as [chapters](/export/chapters/), and the file is written with fast start, so a player can begin before all of it has arrived.
40	
41	## Audio only (WAV)
42	
43	A `.wav` file of uncompressed sound, 48 kHz stereo. Choose it when the mix is going into someone else's tool, where a second round of lossy compression is the one thing you can't take back.
44	
45	It's 16-bit by default, or 24-bit through [Bit depth](/export/bit-depth/). That's about 11.5 MB a minute at 16 bits and 17.3 MB a minute at 24. The footnote reads `LPCM · WAV`, with `24-bit` added at that depth.
46	
47	A WAV holds no chapters, so chapter markers are left out.
48	
49	## Audio only (AIFF)
50	
51	The same samples as a WAV, in an `.aiff` file. WAV stores each sample little-endian and AIFF big-endian, which matters only to the software reading the file, so choose whichever your tool asks for.
52	
53	Everything else is as for WAV: 48 kHz stereo, 16 or 24 bits, the same file size and no chapters. The footnote reads `LPCM · AIFF`.
54	
55	## Which controls apply
56	
57	A control an audio format can't use is greyed out. It keeps what it shows, and nothing from it reaches the file.
58	
59	| Control | M4A | WAV and AIFF |
60	| --- | --- | --- |
61	| **Quality** | Sets the AAC rate | Greyed out |
62	| **Bit depth** | Greyed out | 16-bit or 24-bit |
63	| [**Stems**](/export/stems/) | Available | Available |
64	| [**Loudness**](/export/loudness/) | Available | Available |
65	| [**Range**](/export/range/) | Available | Available |
66	| **Size**, **Frame rate**, **Speed**, **Burn in timecode** | Greyed out | Greyed out |
67	
68	**Size** has nothing to set because there's no picture. A preset saved from an audio format stores no size, so it can't carry one over to a movie.
69	
70	## The 48 kHz stereo master
71	
72	Every export with sound, movies included, reads the mix once as 48 kHz stereo at 32-bit float, and rounds it once at the very end. In between, the loudness gain and the limiter both work on the float mix, so nothing has been clipped before they act.
73	
74	The limiter holds the file's true peak under −1 dBTP. See [Export loudness](/export/loudness/). Sound under that ceiling passes through unchanged.
75	
76	The final rounding goes to the nearest value at the file's bit depth, with no dither at 16 or 24 bits.
77	
78	There's no control for the sample rate or the channel count. Whatever your sources are, the file is 48 kHz stereo.
79	
80	## Good to know
81	
82	- A timeline with no sound at all can't be exported as audio. The export stops with "There is nothing on the timeline to export — add a clip first."
83	- [Stems](/export/stems/) skip the master's limiter, so a stem can peak higher than the mix.
84	- When the export finishes, the sheet reports what the sound measured. See [Export progress and the report](/export/progress-and-report/).
85	
86	## With an agent
87	
88	An agent passes `audio_m4a`, `audio_wav` or `audio_aiff` as the `preset` of `export`. It sets the M4A's rate with `audio_bitrate` and a WAV or AIFF's depth with `audio_bits`. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).
89	
90	## Related

93	- [Export bit depth](/export/bit-depth/)
94	- [Audio stems](/export/stems/)
95	- [Export loudness](/export/loudness/)

101	---
102	
103	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
104	
105	Burn in timecode draws the project's timecode into the exported picture. Use it for a review copy, so a note about a frame carries the number you'll find on your timeline.
106	
107	<AtAGlance
108	  menu="File ▸ Export…"

114	## Burn in timecode
115	
116	Choose **File ▸ Export…** and turn on **Burn in timecode**. It's off by default.
117	
118	The timecode appears only in the exported file, never in the preview. It sits centred near the bottom of the picture, on a translucent black plate, on top of everything, captions included.
119	
120	The box works on every format with a picture, Animated GIF and Animated PNG included. It's greyed out for the audio-only formats, and **File ▸ Save Frame…** never offers it.
121	
122	The sheet remembers it with the rest of your last export, and a [preset](/export/presets/) stores it.
123	
124	## What the timecode shows
125	
126	It uses the project's own timecode format, as the toolbar shows it: `HH:MM:SS:FF` or `HH:MM:SS.mmm`, non-drop. See [Canvas background and timecode](/projects/background-and-timecode/).
127	
128	It shows **project time**. A file exported from an [in/out range](/export/range/) that starts at 00:00:10:00 begins at 00:00 in a player, but its first frame reads 00:00:10:00. That's the number a reviewer's note needs.
129	
130	## With an agent
131	
132	`burn_in_timecode` turns it on in `export`, and it's off by default. `render_frame` takes the same argument, so an agent can draw the timecode into a single frame, which **Save Frame…** can't do. See [Check the picture: render_frame](/mcp/render-frame/).

140	=================== chapters
141	---
142	title: "Chapters"
143	description: "Turn chapter markers into chapters in exported MP4, MOV, M4A and WebM files, and see how a range export treats them."
144	---
145	
146	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
147	
148	Chapters let someone jump through a long video in their player. In Frame Job they come from markers with **Chapter** turned on, with nothing to set on the export sheet.
149	
150	<AtAGlance where="Document tab ▸ Markers ▸ Chapter" tools={['export', 'add_marker', 'set_marker']} />
151	
152	## Chapters in exports
153	
154	[Mark a chapter](/timeline/markers/#make-a-chapter) on the timeline, then export to any format that writes an MP4, MOV, M4A or WebM file. Chapter markers become the file's chapters, in time order.
155	
156	- **Names.** A chapter takes its marker's name. An unnamed marker becomes "Chapter 1", "Chapter 2" and so on, counted over the chapter markers only, so removing a plain marker never renumbers them. A name of only spaces counts as unnamed.
157	- **Lengths.** Each chapter runs to the next one, and the last runs to the end of the file. Time before the first chapter marker belongs to no chapter, so put a marker on the first frame if you want the file to open in one.
158	- **Queued jobs.** A job writes the chapters the timeline had when you confirmed it, whatever you do to the markers afterwards. See [A queued job's snapshot](/export/export-queue/#a-queued-jobs-snapshot).
159	
160	WAV, AIFF, Animated GIF and Animated PNG files have no chapters. Neither do [stems](/export/stems/): only the mix carries them.
161	
162	## Chapters in a range export
163	
164	An [export of a range](/export/range/) keeps the chapters inside the range, with their times counted from the start of the file. The chapter already running when the range starts opens the file, and a chapter starting at or after the range's end is left out.
165	
166	Say the timeline has chapters at 0:00, 1:00 and 3:00, named Intro, Demo and Outro, and you export from 2:00 to 4:00. The file has two chapters: Demo at 0:00 and Outro at 1:00.
167	
168	An unnamed chapter keeps its number from the whole timeline, so the third chapter marker is still "Chapter 3" in a file that holds only two.
169

173	- [Export a range](/export/range/)

175	- [What an export includes](/export/what-an-export-includes/)
176	=================== export-queue
177	---
178	title: "The Export Queue"
179	description: "Write exports behind the editor, one at a time, while you keep working, and follow, cancel or reveal each one from a single window."
180	---
181	
182	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
183	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
184	
185	The Export Queue writes the same file as **Export…** without making you wait for it. Jobs run one at a time behind the editor while you keep working.
186	
187	<AtAGlance
188	  menu="Window ▸ Export Queue"
189	  where="Export sheet ▸ Add to Queue"
190	  tools={['export', 'export_status', 'cancel_export']}
191	/>
192	
193	## Add to Queue
194	
195	<Steps>
196	
197	1. Set up the file in the [export sheet](/export/export-sheet/).
198	
199	2. Choose **Add to Queue**. It's available whenever **Export…** is.
200	
201	3. Name the file in the save panel and choose **Save**. This is the same panel **Export…** opens.
202	
203	</Steps>
204	
205	The **Export Queue** window then opens on its own, with the job in it. Your settings are remembered as the last choice, as they are for **Export…**.
206	
207	Opening the export sheet pauses playback whichever button you use, but after **Add to Queue** no progress sheet is in the way. You can start playback again and go on editing while the job runs.
208	
209	## The Export Queue window
210	
211	Choose **Window ▸ Export Queue** to open it at any time. It has no keyboard shortcut.
212	
213	The window lists every queued, running and finished export. Jobs run one at a time, in the order they were added, unless a job has to [wait for memory](#the-encoder-memory-wait). Closing the window stops nothing. Open it again and the jobs are where they'd got to.
214	
215	The line at the bottom counts the jobs, for example "1 exporting · 2 waiting · 3 finished". With nothing in the list, the window reads "Nothing queued. The Export card's Add to Queue button puts a confirmed export here instead of waiting for it, and they run one at a time while you keep editing."
216	
217	The list isn't saved. It starts empty each time you open Frame Job.
218	
219	## Rows and their states
220	
221	Each row shows the file's name and where the job has got to.
222	
223	| The row says | What it means | Button |
224	| --- | --- | --- |
225	| `Waiting` | Queued behind the running job. | **Cancel** |
226	| `Waiting for memory: …` | An AV1 or VP9 job [waiting for memory](#the-encoder-memory-wait). | **Cancel** |
227	| `Writing · 42 %` | The job is running, with a progress bar beside it. It can stay at `Writing · 0 %` while the job [waits for what it needs](/export/what-an-export-includes/#waiting-for-what-it-needs). | **Cancel** |
228	| `Measuring loudness… · 12 %` | The job is measuring the mix before it writes. | **Cancel** |
229	| `Stopping…` | You cancelled the job and it hasn't stopped yet. | **Cancel** |
230	| `Exported “Board.mp4”.` | The file was written. Any stems, graphic warnings and cursor warnings are counted after the name, then come the [loudness figures](/export/progress-and-report/). | **Show**, **Remove** |
231	| `Overwritten by a later export to the same file.` | The job finished, but a later job has since started writing to the same path. | **Remove** |
232	| `Cancelled.` | You stopped it while it ran. | **Remove** |
233	| `Cancelled before it started.` | You stopped it while it waited. | **Remove** |
234	| The reason it failed | The job stopped with an error. | **Remove** |
235	
236	Hold the pointer over a row for its tooltip: the full path, the container, the size and the frame rate, then the whole memory sentence while a job waits for memory, then each graphic and cursor warning.
237	
238	| Button | What it does |
239	| --- | --- |
240	| **Cancel** | Stops that job and removes its half-written file. A waiting job is cancelled before it starts. |
241	| **Remove** | Takes a finished row out of the list. The file stays where it is. |
242	| **Show** | Reveals the finished file in the Finder. If the file has since been moved or deleted, Frame Job beeps. |
243	
244	## Clear Finished and Cancel All
245	
246	**Clear Finished** removes every finished, cancelled and failed row and leaves the queue running. It's dimmed when there's nothing to clear, and it deletes no files.
247	
248	**Cancel All** stops the running job and every waiting one. It's dimmed when nothing is running or waiting.
249	
250	A cancelled job's half-written file is removed. The queue doesn't delete a failed job's file, so a part-written file can be left where you saved it.
251	
252	## A queued job's snapshot
253	
254	A job holds the timeline as it was when you chose **Save** in the save panel, including its media files, reversed clips, graphics, chapters and any timecode burn-in.
255	
256	Edits, undos and relinks made afterwards don't change what it writes, and neither does closing the document. You can queue one version, go on cutting, and queue another.
257	
258	## Quit with jobs in the queue
259	
260	Quitting while a queued job runs or waits asks first, after Frame Job has asked about any unsaved documents.
261	
262	The alert reads "An export is still being written." and names the running file, for example "“Board.mp4” is not finished, and 2 more are waiting. Quitting now stops it and deletes the partly written file."
263	
264	- **Quit Anyway** cancels the queue, deletes the partly written file and quits.
265	- **Cancel** keeps Frame Job open and the queue running.
266	
267	:::caution
268	Only the queue is guarded this way. Quitting while an **Export…** progress sheet is writing doesn't ask, and leaves the half-written file behind. Cancel that export first.
269	:::
270	
271	## The encoder memory wait
272	
273	AV1 and VP9 are encoded in software, and they use a lot of memory.
274	
275	| Format | At 1080p | At 4K |
276	| --- | --- | --- |
277	| AV1 (MP4) and AV1 (WebM), depending on [Speed](/export/encoder-speed/) | About 1.2–2.4 GB | About 4.4–8.1 GB |
278	| VP9 (WebM) | About 0.4–0.5 GB | About 1.1–1.6 GB |
279	| VP9 with Alpha (WebM) | About 0.7 GB | About 2.2 GB |
280	
281	All the AV1 and VP9 exports running in Frame Job, from the queue and from **Export…** progress sheets, may hold up to a quarter of the Mac's memory together. On a 16 GB Mac that's 4.0 GB.
282	
283	A queued AV1 or VP9 job starts only if it fits in that quarter with what's already running. The queue itself runs one job at a time, so what holds a job back is an AV1 or VP9 export running behind an **Export…** progress sheet.
284	
285	- When nothing else is running, a job always starts, however large.
286	- While a job waits, a later job that fits runs first, and so does any job in a format the Mac encodes itself, such as H.264 or ProRes.
287	- An **Export…** sheet never waits. It's counted and starts straight away, so several sheets at once can go past the quarter.
288	
289	The row's status is one line, so the sentence usually ends in "…" before its figures. The tooltip ends with all of it: "Waiting for memory: AV1 and VP9 exports running now hold about 2.3 GB of the 4.0 GB this Mac allows them, and this one needs about 2.2 GB."
290	
291	The figures are measured, not a guarantee: a heavier timeline can use more.
292	
293	## Good to know
294	
295	- **Export…** doesn't join the queue. It writes straight away behind its [own progress sheet](/export/progress-and-report/), and it can run while a queued job runs.
296	- Two jobs can name the same file. The save panel asks about replacing a file only if it's already on disk, so two quick **Add to Queue** choices with one name may not ask at all. The later job replaces the file as it starts writing, whether or not it goes on to finish, and the earlier row stops offering **Show**.
297	
298	## With an agent
299	
300	An agent's `export` always goes through the queue, never a progress sheet. Its job is a row like any other, but the window doesn't open on its own. `export_status` reads that row, including the memory sentence while the job waits, and `cancel_export` is its **Cancel**, though a running job can still read `running` until writing has stopped. An agent can follow and stop only the jobs it started. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).

308	=================== loudness
309	---
310	title: "Export loudness"
311	description: Normalise a whole mix to a loudness target, and read what every export reports about its sound.
312	---
313	
314	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
315	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
316	
317	Streaming services, podcast hosts and broadcasters each ask for a certain loudness. **Loudness:** on the export sheet makes the whole mix land on that target, and every export tells you what its sound measured, whether you normalised it or not.
318	
319	<AtAGlance
320	  menu="File ▸ Export…"
321	  keys="⌘E"
322	  where="Export sheet ▸ Loudness"
323	  tools={['export', 'export_status']}
324	/>
325	
326	## Hit a loudness target
327	
328	<Steps>
329	
330	1. Choose **File ▸ Export…**.
331	
332	2. In **Loudness:**, choose a target. The footnote on the sheet shows it, for example "−14 LUFS".
333	
334	3. Choose **Export…** or **Add to Queue**.
335	
336	4. When the file is done, read [the loudness line](#what-the-loudness-line-means) to see what it measured.
337	
338	</Steps>
339	
340	## The Loudness popup
341	
342	The target is the integrated loudness of the whole mix: one figure for the file from start to end, in LUFS, measured to ITU-R BS.1770-4.
343	
344	| Choice | What it's for |
345	| --- | --- |
346	| **Off** | No normalisation. The export still goes through the master limiter, measures its sound and reports it. |
347	| **−14 LUFS (streaming)** | Where the main streaming services normalise. |
348	| **−16 LUFS** | The usual target for stereo podcasts. |
349	| **−23 LUFS (broadcast)** | EBU R 128 broadcast delivery. |
350	| **Custom…** | Any target you type in the field beside the popup, from −70 to 0 LUFS, to one decimal place. |
351	
352	The popup works on every format with sound, ProRes included. It's greyed out for Animated GIF and Animated PNG, which have no sound.
353	
354	With **Custom…**, the field starts from the target you had chosen, or −14 after **Off**. While it's empty, the sheet says "Type a loudness target in LUFS, or pick one from the list." and **Export…** is greyed out.
355	
356	The sheet remembers your choice with the rest of your last export, and a [preset](/export/presets/) stores it.
357	
358	## How normalisation works
359	
360	The export measures the real mix first, then applies **one gain** to everything. Levels inside the timeline keep their relationship to each other, so a quiet line stays quieter than a loud one.
361	
362	The progress line reads "Measuring loudness…" during this pass. It fills the first tenth of the progress bar on a movie export, and the first half on an audio-only one.
363	
364	The gain is worked out through the master limiter, so the file lands on the target even when its loudest peaks would pass the ceiling. Those peaks are turned down, not the whole mix.
365	
366	The gain can be at most +40 dB, so a target more than 40 dB above the mix lands quieter than you asked. It's rounded to 0.01 dB, so two exports of one project get the same gain.
367	
368	## The master limiter
369	
370	Every export with sound goes through a true-peak limiter, normalised or not. True peak is the highest the sound really reaches, including between samples, and dBTP is its unit. The limiter keeps the file's true peak at or under **−1 dBTP**. A mix that would pass that is limited instead of clipped, whether the cause is loud clips, a crossfade between two loud clips, a nest turned up or an action that raises a clip's volume.
371	
372	- Sound under the ceiling passes through untouched, sample for sample.
373	- The limiter holds the sound back 3.3 ms to see each peak coming, and releases over 100 ms. The export takes that delay back, so the sound stays exactly in sync with the picture.
374	- You can't turn it off, and the sheet fixes the ceiling at −1 dBTP.
375	
376	:::note
377	The preview has no master limiter, so a mix that passes −1 dBTP sounds louder while you edit than it does in the file.
378	:::
379	
380	## Track compressors in the export
381	
382	A track's own [compressor and limiter](/audio/track-dynamics/) run before the master, on that track's sound alone, exactly as you set them. The export plays each such track on its own through them and mixes the tracks afterwards.
383	
384	The measurement for a loudness target hears them too, so the file still lands on the target. A [stem](/export/stems/) of that track includes them.
385	
386	The master is only the loudness gain and the limiter. There's no master compressor or EQ. To compress the whole mix, [nest](/editing/nests/) everything onto one track and give that track a compressor.
387	
388	## What the loudness line means
389	
390	Every export of a file with sound reports what that sound measured, on the [finish line](/export/progress-and-report/#the-finish-report) and in its [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) row.
391	
392	| Line | What it means |
393	| --- | --- |
394	| `Peak −1.0 dBTP · −14.0 LUFS` | The true peak and integrated loudness of the file. |
395	| `Peak … · loudness not measurable` | The sound is too short or too quiet to have a loudness. It needs at least 0.4 s. |
396	| `Silent` | The sound is digital silence. |
397	| `… · peaks limited by 8.6 dB` | The master limiter turned the loudest peak down by that much to hold the ceiling. It appears from 0.05 dB. |
398	| `Peak not measurable (a non-finite sample in the mix)` | A source file holds a sample that isn't a number, so no gain is applied. |
399	
400	A large "peaks limited by" figure on music can be audible. Turn the clips down, or ask for a lower target.
401	
402	## Good to know
403	
404	- Sound with no loudness to measure gets no gain, so a target has no effect on digital silence or on sound that's too short or too quiet.
405	- If the sound can't be measured at all, the file is written without normalisation and the line has no figures. A timeline with no sound at all has none either.
406	- The figures describe the mix. Stems aren't measured, and they get no target or master limiter.
407	
408	## With an agent
409	
410	`export` takes the target as `loudness_lufs`, any value from −70 to 0, and ignores it on `gif` and `apng`.
411	
412	An agent can also choose a different ceiling for the master limiter with `peak_dbtp`, which the sheet doesn't offer. It runs from −20 to 0 dBTP, is −1 when left out, and works with or without a target. 0 dBTP is the loosest, and there's no way to turn the limiter off.
413	
414	`export_status` returns the line's figures as numbers in `loudness`, and `capped_by_gain` says when the +40 dB limit decided the gain. See [The loudness report](/mcp/export/#the-loudness-report).
415

424	=================== presets
425	---
426	title: "Export presets"
427	description: Save the export sheet's choices under a name, and set the whole sheet with one pick in any project.
428	---
429	
430	import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
431	import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
432	
433	A preset is a set of export choices you've saved under a name. Pick it and the whole sheet is set, in any project. It's the quick way back to the export you make every week.
434	
435	<AtAGlance
436	  menu="File ▸ Export…"
437	  keys="⌘E"
438	  where={['Export sheet ▸ Preset', 'Export sheet ▸ the gear beside Preset']}
439	/>
440	
441	## Apply a preset
442	
443	Pick the preset in **Preset:**. Every control is set exactly as if you had clicked it.
444	
445	The first row is **Custom**, then your presets. Picking **Custom** leaves the sheet as it is. The gear beside the popup saves and deletes presets.
446	
447	## Save a preset
448	
449	<Steps>
450	
451	1. Set the sheet the way you want it.
452	
453	2. Click the gear beside **Preset:** and choose **Save…**.
454	
455	3. Type a name and click **Save**, or **Cancel** to save nothing. The name field starts with the name of the preset now chosen.
456	
457	</Steps>
458	
459	Saving under a name that already exists, ignoring case, replaces that preset in its place in the list. New presets go at the end.
460	
461	Frame Job beeps and saves nothing when:
462	
463	- The name is empty.
464	- The name is **Custom**, in any case. It's reserved for the popup's first row.
465	- The sheet has an error, for example an empty custom field.
466	- The presets file can't be written.
467	
468	## Change a preset
469	
470	Apply it, adjust the controls, and save again under the same name. There's no separate rename: to rename a preset, save it under the new name and delete the old one.
471	
472	## Delete a preset
473	
474	Choose the preset in **Preset:**, then choose **Delete** from the gear. **Delete** is available only while a saved preset is chosen, and it doesn't ask you to confirm.
475	
476	The controls keep the preset's values, so **Save…** under the same name puts it back. It returns at the end of the list.
477	
478	## What a preset stores
479	
480	A preset stores the choices on the sheet, not the numbers they resolve to, so it means the same on a project of another size. A preset saved on a 1080p project that says "4K, High" exports at the right 4K size and bit rate on any other project.
481	
482	It stores:
483	
484	- Format
485	- Size row, or the custom size
486	- Frame rate
487	- Quality tier
488	- Loudness
489	- Range
490	- Burn in timecode
491	- Speed
492	- Bit depth
493	- Stems
494	
495	**Dynamic Range** isn't stored.
496	
497	The format decides what a preset can hold. Size, frame rate, quality, loudness and burn-in aren't stored when the format can't use them, so a preset saved on an audio-only format has no size, and one saved on Animated GIF has no loudness. Applying it puts those controls back on their defaults. Speed, Bit depth and Stems are stored whichever format is chosen.
498	
499	When a preset meets a different project:
500	
501	- A range falls back to **Whole project** if the project has no range.
502	- A size row hidden on this project, because an earlier row has the same numbers, lands on that earlier row. A size row the format doesn't offer falls back to the format's default.
503	- A custom size stays those exact numbers.
504	
505	## Back to Custom
506	
507	Changing **Format:**, **Size:**, **Frame rate:**, **Quality:**, **Loudness:**, **Range:**, **Burn in timecode** or a custom field puts the popup back on **Custom**. Changing the value back doesn't select the preset again.
508	
509	**Speed:**, **Bit depth:** and **Stems:** don't do this. After you change one of those three, the popup still shows the preset's name, even though the sheet no longer matches it.
510	
511	The popup opens on **Custom** each time, even when your remembered choices happen to match a preset.
512	
513	## The presets file
514	
515	Presets are kept for your macOS user account, so every project and window shares them. They live in `~/Library/Application Support/Frame Job/ExportPresets.json`.
516	
517	You can open the file in a text editor. A damaged file reads as no presets, and the export sheet works as usual.
518	
519	Saving or deleting reads the file first, so two open sheets can't lose each other's presets. A sheet that's already open keeps listing a preset you've deleted elsewhere until it saves or deletes a preset itself, or you open it again.
520	
521	## Transparent presets
522	
523	A preset on a transparent format, such as **ProRes 4444 (MOV)** or **HEVC with Alpha (MOV)**, stores the format and nothing about the canvas. The file is transparent only when the project's canvas background is. A custom size also has to match the canvas's shape on these formats, so a preset with a custom size can fail on a canvas of another shape. Use a size row instead, because the rows fit each project's shape. See [Transparent exports](/export/transparency/).
524	
525	## With an agent
526	
527	Presets belong to the sheet, and `export` doesn't read them. Its `preset` argument is something else: it names the format, and the call sets each other choice itself. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).
528
